Annoying Habits That Are Actually Cries for Help

📅 14 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1377 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dogster

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that dogster is reader-supported.
  • Sources indicate that dogs are easy to love but, on occasion, are also surprisingly difficult to live with.
  • Industry observers note that most dog owners have dealt with at least one of these behaviors, and itâs tempting to see them simply as bad habits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

Sources indicate that dogs are easy to love but, on occasion, are also surprisingly difficult to live with. Barking for no reason. The leash pulling that turns a simple walk into a tug-of-war. Turning the most expensive thing in the room into a chew toyâ¦.

Industry observers note that most dog owners have dealt with at least one of these behaviors, and itâs tempting to see them simply as bad habits. But the truth is, there is often a reason behind these irritating habits. Dogs communicate through behavior, and what looks like a nuisance is sometimes a symptom of an unmet need. The trouble is that we often get distracted by tackling that symptom when we really need to dig deeper.

Understanding what is driving an annoying or unwanted behavior can make it much easier to address.

Sources indicate that dogs bark for many reasons, including boredom, anxiety, fear, a perceived threat, or a desire for attention. Any dog can develop a barking habit, regardless of size.

In a recent development, the key is identifying what triggers it. Boredom-related barking may improve with more exercise and mental stimulation, while anxiety or fear-based barking generally requires a more structured approach. Teaching a reliable "quiet" command and avoiding accidentally rewarding attention-seeking barking can also help.

In a recent development, naturally vigilant dogs that spend their days standing guard at windows and alerting you to every passerby or suspicious-looking trash can may become less anxious if you block or obscure their view of the street. Limiting access to front-facing rooms or applying privacy film to windows can be a simple solution â if they canât see it, they stop worrying about it.

Chewing is normal for dogs, particularly teething puppies, but it becomes a problem when furniture, clothing, carpets, or walls become the preferred targets.

Boredom and anxiety can contribute to destructive chewing, as can a lack of appropriate outlets. Keeping suitable chew toys available, putting valuable items out of reach, and managing the environment while the dog learns what is acceptable can help redirect the habit.

A dog that greets visitors by launching itself at them has usually learned that jumping gets a response. Even pushing the dog away or telling it to stop can give them the attention theyâre seeking.

Ignoring the jumping and rewarding calm, four-paws-on-the-floor behavior teaches the dog that staying down gets the better response. Giving the dog an alternative behavior, such as sitting, can make the lesson clearer.

When faced with a friendly jumping dog, try the following:.

Keep your arms crossed, mouth closed, and eyes averted.

Turn your back, and walk away if they keep jumping.

Ignore them until they are calm and ready to listen to your command.

Recent findings suggest that dogs beg because it has worked before. Even one successful attempt at getting food from the table can establish the habit, making it particularly difficult to break.

Feeding the dog before your mealtimes can reduce the motivation to beg, while teaching it to settle in a designated spot gives it something else to do. The biggest challenge is consistency. Giving in occasionally can keep the behavior going.

Table scraps can also pose health risks because some common human foods are harmful to dogs, while regular extras can contribute to obesity.

Sources indicate that leash pulling can make an otherwise enjoyable walk exhausting. Dogs often pull because they are excited and have not learned that pulling does not make the walk happen faster.

Recent findings suggest that loose-leash training takes patience. Stopping whenever the leash becomes tight and continuing only when it becomes slack teaches the dog what behavior allows the walk to continue. Rewarding the dog for walking beside the handler can reinforce the lesson, while a well-fitted harness may provide additional control during training.

According to recent reports, different dogs need different equipment, and what works for a small dog is not necessarily going to be suitable for a large one. Talk to your vet about the safest and most effective option for you and your dog.

Poor recall is frustrating, but it can also be dangerous if your dog runs towards traffic or another dog.

Training should start in areas with few distractions before gradually becoming more challenging. High-value rewards can make coming back more appealing, while using the recall command for unpleasant situations can create a negative association that undermines the training.

Recent findings suggest that digging is instinctive for many dogs and can also be linked to boredom or excess energy. Trying to eliminate the behavior completely may not be the most practical approach; redirection has a much higher chance of success.

Create a designated digging area, such as a sandbox or corner of the yard, making sure there is a clear distinction between this and the rest of the garden. It may be unsightly, but laying down some temporary netting or a similar obstacle in the rest of the yard can help teach your dog where they can and cannot dig. Burying toys or treats there can make the spot more appealing, while increasing daily activity may reduce the urge to dig elsewhere.

Sources indicate that some dogs struggle when left alone. The resulting distress can include destructive behavior, excessive barking, and other difficult behaviors.

According to recent reports, gradually getting a dog used to being alone, starting with very short absences and slowly increasing them, is an evidence-based approach. Providing a comfortable, safe space can also help.

Sources indicate that avoid making a fuss of your dog when leaving the house or on your return â your comings and goings should become part of an ordinary day, not an event. More severe cases of separation anxiety may require veterinary input or help from a behaviorist.

Aggression can have many possible causes, including fear, poor socialization, pain, territorial behavior, or negative past experiences. Because the appropriate response depends on the cause, this is one behavior where professional help is particularly important.

Recent findings suggest that A veterinary examination can help rule out an underlying medical problem, including pain. A qualified trainer or behaviorist can then help address the behavior using approaches such as positive reinforcement, desensitization, and counterconditioning. Punishment can make aggression worse rather than better.

Occasional accidents can happen, but frequent or sudden indoor elimination deserves attention.

For dogs that are still learning, regular bathroom breaks and immediate positive reinforcement for going outside provide the foundation for housetraining. Enzymatic cleaners are useful for removing waste odors that can otherwise encourage a dog to return to the same spot.

If a previously house-trained dog suddenly begins having accidents, a check-up at the vet is appropriate to check for a possible medical cause.

It has been revealed that barking, chewing, jumping, digging, and the other behaviors on this list may be frustrating, but they rarely happen without a reason. Looking at what a dog is trying to communicate can reveal whether it needs more activity, clearer training, or a different kind of attention.

Addressing the underlying matter rather than simply trying to stop the behavior can make the problem easier to manage and help strengthen the relationship between you and your dog.

The Festive Container Plant That Outshines Poinsettias – It's Evergreen And Smells Just Like Vanilla!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I know, I know; poinsettias are absolutely the traditional choice for festive decorating, but there's another festive container plant that deserves a place by your front door this winter.

One of those underrated beauties that deserves its time in the spotlight, this holiday plant may not have the bold and colorful bracts of a classic poinsettia, but what it lacks in showy flowers, it more than makes up for in fragrance, evergreen foliage and year-round appeal.

In fact, if you're looking for a festive container plant that keeps on giving long after the holiday decorations have come down, it could be just the thing you're looking for (and then some!).

Sources indicate that poinsettias are practically synonymous with the holidays, and little wonder; their bright red, pink or white foliage brings an instant splash of festive color. Still, there's no getting away from the fact that their appeal is largely seasonal. They're tender plants, usually grown indoors in the US, and need warmth, bright indirect light, careful watering, and lots of TLC to keep them looking their best.

Industry observers note that once the holidays are over and those colorful bracts begin to fade, many poinsettias end up in the compost or trash. And, while it's possible to keep them growing and even encourage them to develop their colorful bracts again the following year, doing so takes a little effort.

Enter stage left, then, the beautiful sweet box (Sarcococca).

Obviously, sweet box offers a rather different proposition, as this handsome evergreen shrub doesn't have to be replaced when Christmas is over. In fact, its glossy leaves provide structure and greenery throughout the year, while its winter flowers bring a welcome surprise just when the garden can feel at its dullest.

According to recent reports, and it's not just about looks, either! Sweet box has a secret weapon that poinsettias simply can't compete with: its extraordinary perfume.

That's right, folks; sweet box produces masses of creamy-white flowers in winter, often tucked discreetly beneath its glossy leaves. They might not look particularly impressive from a distance, but get close and you'll discover why this shrub is so treasured, as they release a perfume often described as a combination of vanilla and jasmine.

It's surprisingly powerful for such delicate blooms, and on a still winter day, the scent can drift through the garden and greet you as you approach your front door. Especially if you opt for a variety like the Sweet & Lo™ Sweet Box from Proven Winners.

Once flowering finishes, sweet box can produce ornamental berries, which mature from red to dark purple or black depending on the species and variety. And it does all of this while standing in partial or full shade, no less!

Recent findings suggest that although some sweet box varieties can eventually become quite substantial shrubs, its slow-growing nature also makes it a useful long-term container plant. (You won't be constantly battling to keep it in shape, for starters, although a light trim after flowering can help maintain a neat outline if needed).

In a recent development, just be sure to choose a pot with drainage holes and use a good moisture-retentive potting mix. Pop it somewhere sheltered in partial or full shade, and water when the compost begins to dry – just like all container-grown plants, it will need a little more attention to watering than those growing in the ground, particularly during dry spells.

Recent findings suggest that of course, there's nothing wrong with a beautiful poinsettia, but if you'd rather invest in a plant that offers more than a few weeks of seasonal color, sweet box is well worth your time... not to mention a place in your heart. Not least of all because it's the sort of hard-working hero plant that continues to provide beauty long after the festive season has passed.

In a recent development, if your home and garden is full of those awkward shady spots where other plants might struggle, then, look no further! And if not? Well, still show it some love, I say – for a festive container with fragrance, character and staying power, sweet box is a very hard plant to beat.

As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

Last-Minute Bulbs to Plant in November

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (421 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that fall-planted bulbs that flower in spring are surely the easiest, cheapest way to add color to your garden.
  • Recent findings suggest that when you’re planting bulbs in late fall, the secret to success is great drainage so they root rather than rot.
  • Industry observers note that if it’s a while since you went bulb shopping, you’re in for a lovely surprise because plant breeders have been busy creating all sorts of wonderful new flower shapes and color combinations.

It has been revealed that fall-planted bulbs that flower in spring are surely the easiest, cheapest way to add color to your garden. Pop the bulbs into the ground in fall, then do absolutely nothing at all until green stems pierce the cold spring soil to light up your yard with fabulous flowers. From tulips to crocus, hyacinths to Dutch iris, there are plenty of showstopper bulbs you can still plant in November. As long as your ground isn’t frozen or waterlogged, all these beauties can be planted now, at a depth that's three times the bulb's height. If you live in a colder USDA zone and already past your first frost date, simply plant bulbs in a container in a sheltered spot instead.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re planting bulbs in late fall, the secret to success is great drainage so they root rather than rot. That’s easily done by giving bulbs an inch-deep layer of grit to sit on at the base of the planting hole. You could fork out on horticultural grit, or you could simply use good ol’ poultry grit made of crushed granite like CZ Grain Chicken Grit, available from Walmart. You may need to protect tasty tulip bulbs from hungry squirrels, but then you can leave the rest to Mother Nature.

Industry observers note that if it’s a while since you went bulb shopping, you’re in for a lovely surprise because plant breeders have been busy creating all sorts of wonderful new flower shapes and color combinations. From double-petalled tulips that look just like peonies to fragrant hyacinths in dramatic hues, these backyard blooms are a real springtime treat and planting them should be on everyone's list of gardening jobs in November. So let's skip straight to the good bit, shall we? Here’s my pick of dazzling spring-flowering bulbs to plant in late fall. Get the drainage right and all these will return year in, year out and with prices from 35 cents a bulb, there’s an option to suit every budget.

Breaking: What Your Orchid Needs in November for Spectacular Winter Blooms – 6 Easy Tasks to Do Now

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sometime in early November, a moth orchid (Phalaenopsis) on the windowsill might push out upcoming growth.
  • All of this happens right as basic orchid care gets harder, too.
  • Industry observers note that thankfully, you don't need to do anything dramatic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometime in early November, a moth orchid (Phalaenopsis) on the windowsill might push out upcoming growth. It could be a root, but it could also be the start of a flower spike – and that's why orchids in November deserve a closer look than they got all summer.

All of this happens right as basic orchid care gets harder, too. The days are shorter, and less light gets through the glass. The furnace has kicked on by now, drying out the indoor air, and the bark in the pot stays wet much longer than it did in July. Roots left sitting wet can go soft. Buds sometimes yellow and drop off before they open.

Industry observers note that thankfully, you don't need to do anything dramatic. Most of it is moving a pot a little closer to the window, feeling the bark before you water, or shifting the plant out of a draft. Changes made now, while spikes are just getting started, give a moth orchid a better shot at a full display later in winter or into spring.

It has been revealed that cooler fall temperatures are the main trigger for flower spikes in moth orchids, and shorter days may help a little, so this is the month when plenty of growers start spotting them. The trouble is, spikes and aerial orchid roots look a lot alike when they first poke out. Look closely at the tip, and you can usually tell. Roots come to a bit of a point. Back from the tip, they're wrapped in a spongy layer that goes silvery when it's dry and turns green after you water. Spikes don't have that coating at all. They're green the whole way up, and the end is rounded and closed off, kind of like a mitten.

Before attempting to train a latest orchid flower spike, give it some time to grow on its own first. When it's several inches long, push a stake into the bark close to the base. Angle it a little so you don't spear a root. Then clip the spike to it loosely, adding another clip higher up every so often as it grows. Orchid flowers don't always grow completely straight, so you may have more success with bendable stakes, like these Sproot stakes with clips on Amazon.

Flowers might still be a couple of months off, or longer, so Christmas blooms on every plant aren't a sure thing. Once buds show, quit turning the pot around – they'll grow toward whatever light they're getting.

That shady spot that kept a moth orchid from scorching in July can be too dim by November. Low light can keep a mature plant from spiking at all, and it can also cause bud drop later on.

Industry observers note that an east window is a good choice right now to meet your orchid's light requirements. South and west windows work too, as long as a sheer curtain softens the harshest afternoon sun – direct rays can still overheat buds and burn leaves.

Watch the glass, though. On a frosty night, a pane can get cold enough to damage a leaf resting against it, so leave some space between the plant and the window. Not every house has a sunny window open for one more pot, and a grow light can make up for that. This Sansi clip-on grow light clips right onto the pot.

Recent findings suggest that bark that dried out in no time over the summer can hang onto water much longer in a cool, dim room. Often, orchids get into trouble on a fixed watering schedule this time of year.

Sources indicate that so how do you know when it's time to water orchids? Look at the roots. Silvery, whitish roots are dry, and green ones still have water in them. Lift the pot to feel its weight, too, since a light one is another clue.

In a recent development, clear plastic orchid pots, like these from Walmart, make it easier to check. Moisture meters are less reliable with orchids, but some growers like to use a Sustee Aquameter stick for a second opinion. It turns white once the mix dries out.

When it is time to water, give it a real soak. Take the pot to the sink and run room-temperature water through it till it pours out the bottom. Let it drain all the way. If any water is sitting where the leaves meet, tip it out.

Bark tells you more, honestly, than the calendar will. But bone-dry all winter is the wrong move. Moth orchids don't go dormant, and roots that sit dry for weeks can shrivel.

Kept warm around the clock, a moth orchid can go on growing leaves for months without sending up a spike. That seems a little backward, if you think about it, for a tropical plant. Cooler temperatures encourage flower spikes, and nights around 60–65°F (16–18°C) for a few weeks in fall can help. Daytime heat matters too, and a spot by a heat vent that keeps the plant much above 80°F (27°C) for long stretches can hold spiking back.

Cooler doesn't mean cold. Try to keep moth orchids above about 55°F (13°C), and don't park them by an outside door or a leaky window.

Industry observers note that after buds form, forget about the temperature drop. Steady conditions matter more at that point. A cold blast every time the door opens can make buds yellow and fall before they open, and so can hot air blowing off a register.

Growth slows down this month, and slower growth uses less fertilizer. How much to cut back depends on the plant and where it's sitting. Under a grow light in a warm room, a moth orchid may still be making latest leaves and roots. On a cool windowsill, it might barely grow at all.

Other types of orchids are a different story, and a few kinds need a drier, leaner rest through winter – check the type before you change anything.

Not feeding at all is its own kind of mistake, though, just a quieter one. Moth orchids cut off from fertilizer while spikes form or flowers open can end up with fewer blooms. A diluted dose of an all-purpose orchid fertilizer, mixed as directed on the label, keeps them going. One option is Better-Gro Orchid Plus, available at Walmart, a 20-14-13 formula sold in a 1-pound (454 g) bag.

Bloom boosters aren't the shortcut they sound like. Moth orchids fed a balanced formula will often produce more flowers than those given high-phosphorus fertilizer.

According to recent reports, bud blast is the term growers use when buds turn yellow and fall off before they open. Heating season brings plenty of the usual causes. Dry furnace air is one. So is a radiator sitting too close, or a cold draft every time the door opens. Bark that keeps swinging from soaked to bone dry doesn't help either.

Fruit on the counter is a sneaky one, oddly enough – as it ripens, it gives off ethylene gas that can make buds drop, so keep budded orchids away from the fruit bowl.

According to recent reports, damp pebbles in a tray under the pot raise the humidity a little, like this Brussel's humidity tray with decorative rocks. In a very dry room, a small humidifier, like this compact Pure Enrichment MistAire Studio humidifier, adds moisture without taking up much space.

According to recent reports, while you're watering, look the plant over for orchid pests. Mealybugs usually turn up on the spike or where a leaf joins the stem. Something that looks like a bit of white cotton stuck in there is probably the long-tailed mealybug (Pseudococcus longispinus) or citrus mealybug (Planococcus citri). Boisduval scale (Diaspis boisduvalii) looks nothing like that. You'll find it as small, flat bumps on the leaves, almost like they're part of the plant. Both pests weaken an orchid and spread to others nearby.

Industry observers note that wipe off the ones you can see with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol. If they keep coming back, switch to an insecticidal soap or horticultural oil labeled for orchids. Safer Brand Insect Killing Soap, available at Walmart, is one option that targets mealybugs and other common houseplant pests. Test a small area first, then repeat treatment as directed on the label to catch newly hatched pests.

Routine orchid repotting can wait. It's easier on the plant when fresh roots are actively growing, often after flowering finishes, and root disturbance while a spike develops can set it back. The exception is bark that's broken down into mush or roots that have gone brown and soft – that plant needs fresh mix now, spike or no spike.

Sources indicate that leave healthy green spikes alone, too. One without buds yet may still flower, and there's no sense tossing away blooms you might've had. Cold glass is another one to watch on the coldest nights, so pull the leaves back if they're touching the window. Then there's the crown, where the upcoming leaves come out of the center. Water that sits in there can cause crown rot. If that rot reaches the growing point, the plant has no way of making new leaves from the top again.

Most of what an orchid needs in November is a little attention. Spot the upcoming spike, lift the pot before you water, and notice the draft by the back door. Get those right, and there's a good chance of a long run of flowers sometime between midwinter and spring. That's not bad for moving a pot a few feet.

Industry observers note that when my boss passed away, I took in his older Red Heeler, Bob, so he didnât end up in the pound. I've been giving him turkey tail for his lumps, and he is overweight.

Itâs hard to walk him when it's 100 degrees out. For the last couple of months, he has been drinking so much water and urinating way more than usual. He mostly stays inside, and when I take him out to pee, the first thing when he comes back in is head for the water bowl, like he wants to replace what he just got rid of!

Any suggestions on what I could try?â.

Recent findings suggest that you have done something very kind by giving Bob a home after losing his person. It sounds like he is a senior boy who has already been through a lot, and it is wonderful that he has someone looking out for him. The increased drinking and urination you are seeing, especially since this has been going on for a couple of months, is something I would have checked rather than assuming it is just his age or the hot weather. Older dogs can develop several conditions that cause this combination of signs, including diabetes, kidney disease, and Cushing's disease.

I would schedule a veterinary examination and ask for some basic lab work, particularly blood tests and urinalysis. These can give us information that we simply cannot get from looking at Bob. Bloodwork can tell us about his blood glucose, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, and other changes that may help identify what is going on. A urine sample is just as valuable. It can show whether his kidneys are concentrating the urine properly, and can also detect glucose, ketones, protein, blood, inflammation, and other abnormalities. Depending on those results, his veterinarian may recommend some additional tests.

Recent findings suggest that please do not limit his water, even if it seems like he is drinking right back what he just urinated. In many of these conditions, the excessive thirst is the body's way of trying to replace fluid that is being lost. Taking water away can actually make him dehydrated and much sicker. Keep fresh water available at all times, and because of the heat, try to take him out during the cooler parts of the day. If you can, measuring approximately how much water he drinks in 24 hours would also be very helpful information for his veterinarian.

Sources indicate that I would also recommend that he has the lumps properly checked rather than relying on turkey tail or other supplements. Some lumps are harmless, but others can be more serious, and we cannot tell the difference just by feeling or looking at them. A fine needle aspiration can often collect cells from a lump with very little discomfort and may give the veterinarian a much better idea of what it is. With Bob being overweight and having difficulty walking in the heat, getting his medical challenges sorted out first will also make it much safer to work on his weight and mobility.

He has clearly found someone who cares about him, and sometimes the most loving thing we can do for an older dog is simply to find out what his body is trying to tell us.

How to Prepare Your Raised Beds for Winter – 6 Easy Wins for Healthier Soil and Better Harvests Next Year

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1560 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Raised beds are cosy homes for vegetables, annuals and perennials, but, like all homes, they require maintenance.
  • Sources indicate that because raised beds sit above the ground, their soil cools down faster, is more exposed to biting winter wind, and faces heavier nutrient leaching from seasonal downpours.
  • Sources indicate that best of all, these winterizing tasks are quick, low-effort wins.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Raised beds are cosy homes for vegetables, annuals and perennials, but, like all homes, they require maintenance. When you prepare raised beds for winter, you make things easier for all your plants next season. With proper care, you can ensure that your raised bed frames and soils are safe from frost and winter rain, and that any plants you subsequently add can hit the ground running.

Sources indicate that because raised beds sit above the ground, their soil cools down faster, is more exposed to biting winter wind, and faces heavier nutrient leaching from seasonal downpours. Neglected beds may develop drainage issues or lose valuable nutrients. The best raised garden bed ideas protect your soil from winter’s worst. Taking a few simple winter-smart steps now can help to extend the life of the soil, prevent nutrient leaching, and make a strong spring harvest far more likely.

Sources indicate that best of all, these winterizing tasks are quick, low-effort wins. Whether you are tending a single cedar herb box or galvanized steel troughs, prepping your beds now guarantees more fertile soil in spring, earlier planting windows, healthier perennials, and your most bountiful harvests yet. Here’s how to protect your raised beds through winter.

Sources indicate that before you start these tasks, take a quick inventory of your raised bed setup. Size, depth, and construction material can all influence how your beds weather the cold. Wooden beds (like cedar, redwood, or pine) offer natural insulation, but absorb moisture, making them prone to swelling, warping, or fungal rot if soggy debris sits against the boards all winter. You can buy a wood sealant to protect bed frames from winter moisture, as long as it is safe, such as Seal It Green’s Plant-Based Garden Bed Sealer, available from Amazon.

According to recent reports, galvanized metal beds and stone beds are virtually rot-proof, but they conduct cold rapidly. This can mean that soil near the outer walls might freeze and thaw faster, putting perimeter plant roots under extra stress. Shallow beds under 10 inches (25cm) deep can also freeze solid much sooner than deep 18-24-inch (45-60cm) troughs. Bear all this in mind when tackling the jobs here.

Where you live has a part to play, too. In northern regions (USDA hardiness zones 3-6), you need to complete winter prep before the top few inches of soil freeze solid, typically by late November. In milder southern and coastal areas (zones 7-10), winterizing is more about suppressing cool-season weeds, preventing heavy rain from washing away nutrients, and tucking in cold-hardy crops like garlic or kale.

Sources indicate that visit your beds after rainfall to check soil moisture and drainage before beginning your winter tune-up. You can buy a soil temperature and moisture diagnostic tool, such as the Daybetter Soil Meter 4-in-1 from Walmart, to check whether raised bed soil is ready for cover crops or mulch. Then you are ready to get your beds in shape with these tips….

It has been revealed that it used to be standard advice to strip beds bare in fall, but leaving soil naked can expose it to erosion, deplete soil nutrition, and destroy vital overwintering habitats for beneficial pollinators and predatory beetles. Instead, be selective about cleanup. Pull out all spent annual veg and frost-blackened fruiting crops such as tomatoes, peppers, and squash. Also remove persistent weeds. Don’t toss these into the compost pile, but bag them for municipal green waste.

It has been revealed that for healthy, disease-free annuals like beans, peas, or marigolds, snip stems at soil level with clean pruners such as the Felco F2 Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon. Leaving the roots in the ground prevents soil disturbance and feeds earthworms and soil microbes as they decompose over winter. Finally, remove bamboo stakes, tomato cages, and trellises, scrubbing off clinging soil and fungal spores with a mild diluted bleach or vinegar wash before storing them dry.

Sources indicate that intensive raised bed gardening draws heavily on soil reserves over summer, leaving it depleted by November. Replenishing fertility now allows rain, snow, and microbial activity to work on amendments before spring planting begins. Gently loosen any compacted soil using a broadfork or standard garden fork. Push the tines in and rock back slightly. If you need a good fork, the Ames 4-Tine Forged Spading Fork from The Home Depot can help improve drainage without churning up soil structure.

It has been revealed that spread a generous 2-3-inch (5-8cm) layer of aged organic compost, leaf mold, or well-rotted manure across the surface. Avoid hot, uncomposted manure, which can burn roots and leach excess nitrates. If your soil test indicates low phosphorus or acidity (common in high-rainfall regions) then add slow-acting mineral amendments such as rock phosphate, greensand, or garden lime. These require several months to break down and adjust soil chemistry before spring crops go in.

According to recent reports, once your soil is fed, your next mission is to protect the surface from winter erosion, temperature swings, and nutrient washout. Your first option is to tuck the soil under a thick blanket of fluffy organic mulch. For beds lying fallow, or housing perennial herbs and cold-hardy greens, apply a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of shredded fall leaves, clean weed-free straw, or pine needles over your compost layer. Avoid heavy mats of wet grass clippings or unshredded oak leaves, which block oxygen and harbor slugs.

Alternatively, in mild regions, you can sow fast-establishing cover crops like winter rye, crimson clover, hairy vetch, or tillage daikon radish. Their roots help to anchor soil against torrential rain. They also scavenge leftover nitrogen and break up deep compaction, ready to be chopped down and turned 3-4 weeks before spring planting. Buy Outside Pride Crimson Clover Seeds from Amazon for just a few dollars.

Shallow-rooted perennials and newly planted spring bulbs in raised beds face a couple of threats: frost heaving and hungry digging pests. Repeated freezing nights and thawing sunny days can cause wet soil to expand and contract, pushing shallow crowns such as coral bells, foamflowers, and strawberries out of the earth. To prevent frost heave, wait until the ground has frozen lightly. Then mound 3-4 inches (8-10cm) of shredded leaves or evergreen boughs around the crowns. This locks in consistent cold temperatures rather than trapping warmth that delays dormancy.

Industry observers note that raised beds packed with newly planted tulips, crocus, or ranunculus bulbs are very tempting for squirrels, voles, and chipmunks. Lay half-inch hardware cloth or chicken wire flat across the soil surface, weighing down the edges with bricks or landscape staples. If you need a good mesh then Ashman Online Hardware Cloth, available from The Home Depot, can stop squirrels and voles from digging up bulbs. Remove it in early spring as green shoots emerge.

Winter can put structural stress on raised beds, making this the ideal time for a quick inspection. Walk the perimeter and check corner brackets, screws, and timber boards for splitting, wood rot, or rust. Tighten any loose hardware and brace any bowing sides, especially on long wooden beds over 8 feet (2.4m) long. Place a spirit level across the top edges to ensure frames haven't settled unevenly. You can buy Allfun Metal Raised Bed Brackets from Amazon to reinforce ageing or bowing wooden bed corners.

What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

Recent findings suggest that that is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is presently looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

Sources indicate that TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

Industry observers note that rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

The interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

The Dog Aging Projectâs TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

Industry observers note that lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

In a recent development, living longer is great, but what matters just as much is how dogs feel during those extra years. More time with the family means less if a dog is struggling with chronic illness, having trouble getting around, or experiencing cognitive decline. The goal isn't just to add years to a dog's life. It's to help them enjoy more of those years feeling good.

TRIAD is examining several areas of canine health, including cognitive function, heart function, immunity, and cancer incidence.

The current TRIAD recruitment drive is specifically aimed at older dogs that meet the study's eligibility requirements. To be considered for the study, dogs must:.

Be able to cooperate with examinations, including blood collection and cardiac ultrasound, without sedation.

Have normal diagnostic findings at enrollment.

Clinical trial sites are located throughout the United States.

According to recent reports, for families who decide to participate, it is vital to consider that this is a three-year commitment. During the first year, dogs receive either rapamycin or a placebo. Once that year is over, the medication stops, but the study continues. Researchers will follow the dogs for another two years to see how they age and whether any differences emerge over time. In total, owners will bring their dogs to a clinical trial site seven times during the three-year study.

When it comes to getting older, dogs and humans have quite a lot in common. Dogs are susceptible to many of the same age-related conditions we are, including cognitive decline, arthritis, heart disease, cancer, and other chronic health problems. And since they share our homes and daily environments, a great deal of what researchers learn from studying aging in dogs can be extrapolated to humans.

In a recent development, the recent 60 Minutes report touched on this connection, including research into canine dementia. It's an area worth paying attention to, especially as more dogs live into their senior years.

It has been revealed that there's also a practical advantage. Dogs age much faster than humans. This allows researchers to track changes in their health over a few years instead of waiting decades. That's a big deal when you're trying to understand what happens as the body ages.

But this isn't just about what dogs can teach us about ourselves. What researchers discover will help dogs, too.

Aging isn't a single disease that can be treated with one medication. As dogs get older, several things can start changing at once, sometimes as a domino or cascade effect after an initial problem or illness. Maybe getting up becomes harder, walks get shorter, or a dog who's always been sharp seems a little confused. Sometimes these changes happen gradually, and it's easy to chalk them up to old age.

The more we learn about what's actually happening in an aging dog's body, the better chance veterinarians have of spotting problems earlier and finding ways to help dogs feel good for as long as possible.

Due to the eligibility requirements, not every dog will qualify for TRIAD, but that doesnât mean they canât contribute to canine aging research.

The Dog Aging Project also has a broader research community known as the DAP Pack, which welcomes dogs of different ages, sizes, breeds, and backgrounds. The project explains that dogs who do not qualify for TRIAD can still make a meaningful contribution to understanding canine aging.

Itâs notable to include all kinds of dogs in this research, not just a particular breed or size. A dog's genes, lifestyle, environment, size, and even their health history can all play a role in how they age. The more variety researchers can study, the better picture they can get of why some dogs stay healthy well into their senior years while others develop health problems earlier.

In a recent development, when it comes to canine aging, the goal isn't just to help dogs live longer. It's to help them feel good for more of those years, stay active, and keep enjoying life with their families.

And anyone who's lived with a senior dog knows that two dogs of the same age can be worlds apart. One 10-year-old may still be eager for walks, playtime, and whatever the family has planned that day. Another might be struggling with mobility or dealing with several health problems. So, what makes the difference?

It has been revealed that that's part of what makes the TRIAD study interesting. Rapamycin has shown promising results in other species, but researchers still need to find out whether it can make a meaningful difference in dogs. That's a question that needs to be tested, and your pup may be part of this!

Recent findings suggest that for owners of senior dogs, taking part in research like this is a chance to help scientists get some answers. What they learn could help us better understand why dogs age differently and what might help them stay healthier as they get older.

So, if you have a pup in their golden years, check out the Dog Aging Project and see how your four-legged friend might become part of this research.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Late fall is an vital time to prep a garden for winter, and knowing which plants to mulch in November is a vital part of the blueprint. As weather worsens and the ground begins to freeze, adding an insulating layer of mulch keeps soil temperatures more stable, helping plants to survive winter better. Protected from freeze-thaw cycles, frost heaving and low temperatures that could cause root damage, mulched plants will wake up in spring ready for abundant growth.

Because many plants have died down by late fall, mulching in November is a speedy and satisfying job on a crisp sunny day. All you need to do is spread a layer of mulch on top of the soil, keeping it away from the plant stems, which is easy with a hand rake such as this from Lowe's. For best results, choose a mulch made of natural materials like compost, shredded leaves or bark, as it will start breaking down over the winter to supply the soil with nutrients, ready to fuel that strong spring growth.

Sources indicate that many folk like to mulch all their borders when winterizing a garden in fall because it not only protects plants but helps to suppress weeds and keeps beds looking smart over winter. However, while most plants will get through winter better if treated to a fall mulch, there are a few which don't appreciate this extra layer so it's important to know which to leave be. There are a few plants that seriously benefit from a late fall mulch, too, so even if you're not planning on protecting your whole yard, it's well worth mulching these garden heroes. Here's everything you need to know to get great results.

Industry observers note that if you’ve planted upcoming perennials this fall, whether you bought them from a garden center or had success creating free plants by dividing your perennials, they're likely not fully established in their new home yet. This means they're more vulnerable than your other perennials to the cold temperatures and fluctuations of winter weather.

Mulching now is a smart idea for all newly planted perennials, but especially any that are borderline hardy in your growing region. Loosely apply three to four inches (8-10cm) of mulch around these plants as the soil begins to freeze.

Sources indicate that many roses benefit from winter mulching, especially less hardy varieties and those that are newly planted. Fluctuating temperatures can damage plants and cause frost heaving, pushing the roots out of the ground. Mulch roses with 8 to 12 inches (20-30cm) of compost or organic mulch, or even loose, light soil around their bases, keeping the mulching material a couple inches away from the stems of the plants to prevent moisture collection that can trigger rot.

It has been revealed that reliably hardy, well-established hydrangeas may not need mulching but younger plants will benefit from a protective layer this month. Hydrangeas have shallow roots that can be damaged by the cold and the frost heaving that often results from freeze-thaw cycles. Winter damage can stunt spring growth, so a layer of mulch can give your plants a head start next season.

Sources indicate that mulch hydrangeas with two to six inches (5-15cm) of organic material, depending on how cold your winters are. Keep in mind that mulch only protects the roots, so you may also want to protect buds growing on old wood with a burlap wrap during cold snaps.

Sources indicate that your spring bulbs – tulips, crocuses, daffodils and hyacinths – need time to establish roots before winter, and fluctuating soil temperatures can disrupt this process by freezing and thawing repeatedly. The solution is to apply two to three inches of light, loose mulch as the soil begins to freeze. This keeps soil temperatures more consistent, and can also prevent premature emergence during periods of milder winter weather.

If you're adding spring-flowering bulbs that can still be planted in November to your garden – and there are plenty that are fine to go into the soil this late in fall – then mulch straight after planting.

Strawberries are particularly vulnerable to damage caused by cold temperatures but also by the cycles of freezing and thawing that many gardens experience. Cover your strawberry patch with a loose layer of three to four inches of an organic mulch. Weed-free straw such as HealthiStraw GardenStraw, available from Amazon, is a good choice for protecting without compacting and weighing down delicate strawberry plants. Pull the straw back in spring as you see new growth, but leave it around the edges or between rows of plants to keep berries clean and off the ground as they develop.

Recent findings suggest that while many people use mums as fall annuals, there are hardy chrysanthemums that can be grown as perennials with the right care. To get them to come back next year, though, you’ll need to add some mulch for winter protection. They have shallow roots, so the extra insulation helps prevent cold damage. To protect your new garden mums, leave the foliage intact and spread a loose layer of a few inches of organic mulch under and around the leaves.

Always choose a mulch made from natural plant materials, as that will improve your soil as well as protect your plants. Choose undyed mulch to avoid adding unnecessary chemicals to the soil, and there's no need to use mulch binder or glue to keep it in place.

You can buy purpose-made mulch like like Timberline Pine Bark Mulch, stocked by Lowe's, but there are plenty of other options to choose from to suit your garden style and budget. You could use homemade compost or a store-bought compost like Back to the Roots Organic Compost, available from Amazon. Fall leaves that you've shredded by running the lawn mower over a few times make an excellent, free mulch, while bark chips like Golden Trophy Pine Bark Nuggets from Walmartadd texture to your beds.

In a recent development, coco coir chips such as Riare Organic Coco Husk Chips, available from Amazon, are a sustainable option as they're made from outer coconut husks, are a sustainable option. Because they're packaged in a dehydrated form, the bales are compact and light to carry. While coco coir is a very effective mulch, it's not the best option for an exposed garden as after a long dry spell the chips can become light enough to be blown around by strong winds.

All these natural mulches will break down to enrich your soil and improve its structure so it drains freely yet holds onto valuable moisture.

According to recent reports, november is the right time to mulch in many gardens, but it’s important to follow your local conditions when deciding on exact timing, depending on your USDA zone. Applying mulch early might feel like you’re getting ahead, but this can warm the soil too much and delay plants going into dormancy. So, wait until plants are dormant and the ground is beginning to freeze, which typically happens after several hard frosts.

It has been revealed that for all the plants that will thank you for the cozy winter coverage mulch provides, a few can be damaged by it. These plants are vulnerable to excessive moisture, poor airflow, or having their crowns and growth points covered so, while they may benefit from a very light layer of mulch, be careful not to smother them.

According to recent reports, winter mulching is all about strategic protection, not simply covering everything in a thick layer of insulation. But get it right and employ a few insulating frost jackets to zip up vulnerable plants and keep them cozy, and your garden will be protected from the worst of the winter cold, ready to flourish once spring arrives.

Halloween packs a steady stream of costumed strangers and bowls of candy into a single evening, and for dogs that combination carries more hazards than most people expect. Most of the risks are easy to avoid with a little planning, and several of them start well before the first trick-or-treater arrives at the door. These precautions help keep dogs out of trouble while the rest of the household enjoys Halloween.

Halloween candy can be dangerous for dogs, and the wrappers create an additional hazard. Certain ingredients in sweets, including chocolate and xylitol, can be toxic to dogs, while swallowed wrappers can cause choking or digestive problems.

Keeping candy in a closed container at home is a good starting point, but the risk doesn't end at the front door. Keeping a close eye on what a dog sniffs or picks up can help prevent an unwanted snack from turning into a veterinary emergency.

Costumes for dogs can be adorable and hilarious, but only if the dog agrees. Not every dog feels happy playing dress-up, so itâs important to pay attention to how they respond.

Industry observers note that A costume should fit comfortably without restricting movement or creating opportunities for the dog to become tangled. An outfit that fit last year may now be too tight, while one bought for a puppy to grow into could be awkward or unsafe in the meantime.

Before heading out or welcoming visitors, check that the costume fits properly and your pup can walk comfortably in it.

In a recent development, A Halloween costume can look adorable on a dog, but wearing one safely requires supervision. Some dogs become fascinated by their outfits and start chewing at loose fabric or accessories, potentially creating a choking hazard.

There's no reason every dog has to avoid costumes, provided the outfit is comfortable and the dog tolerates wearing it. But if the dog needs to be left alone, take the costume off. It's a simple precaution that reduces the chance of an otherwise harmless outfit causing trouble.

Halloween can be overwhelming for dogs that struggle with noise, unfamiliar people, or constant activity. Trick-or-treaters arrive throughout the evening, and costumes can make even familiar surroundings feel different.

In a recent development, A dog that becomes overexcited or anxious may benefit from having somewhere quiet to retreat. A separate room with a comfortable bed, fresh water, and familiar toys can provide a welcome break from the commotion.

Make sure visitors understand that the dog shouldn't be disturbed if it chooses to settle somewhere away from the activity.

Jack-o'-lanterns, lights, and other Halloween decorations can make a home feel festive, but curious dogs may see them as things to investigate or chew. Keep decorations out of reach, particularly anything that could be harmful if swallowed.

Sources indicate that real candles inside pumpkins also pose a risk if a dog knocks one over. Battery-operated alternatives are a safer choice, especially in areas where pets can wander freely.

Glow sticks and glowing bracelets help make children more visible during evening trick-or-treating, but their bright colors and flexible shapes can also attract a dog's attention.

In a recent development, the liquid inside can cause irritation and may be harmful if swallowed. A dog that bites through a glow stick could end up ingesting the contents, so these items should be kept well away from curious mouths.

Industry observers note that check the ground during walks, too, particularly on Halloween night when discarded glow sticks and bracelets may be lying around. If a dog chews or swallows one, contact a vet for advice.

Handing out candy can mean opening the front door dozens of times in a single evening. For a dog that's curious, excitable, or easily frightened, those repeated opportunities can make an escape more likely.

Sources indicate that closing the door between visitors helps prevent a dog from slipping outside unnoticed. Another option is to step outside to greet trick-or-treaters and close the door behind you.

It has been revealed that keeping the dog in a separate room during busy periods adds another layer of protection. It also reduces the chance of a dog becoming startled by costumed visitors appearing at the entrance.

An identification tag and microchip are always a good idea, but they become particularly crucial on a night when doors are opening frequently, and unusual sights may startle a dog.

In a recent development, if a dog escapes, an ID tag with current contact details gives whoever finds it a straightforward way to get in touch. A microchip provides another means of identifying the dog and helping it return home.

Check that the dog's tag is attached securely and that the contact information associated with its microchip is up to date. These small steps can make a significant difference if a dog gets loose.

In a recent development, halloween can be stressful and dangerous for dogs, but it doesnât have to be. Keeping candy secured, choosing comfortable costumes, providing a quiet retreat, and making sure the front door stays closed can prevent many of the problems associated with the holiday.

It has been revealed that it's also worth remembering that dogs may react unpredictably to unfamiliar costumes and unusual activity, even if they're normally relaxed around visitors. Staying attentive from the first doorbell to the last helps keep the evening enjoyable for everyone, including the four-legged members of the household.

#21351. These 8 Evergreen Plants Make Your Porch Look Magical at Christmas – And They Stay Gorgeous All Winter

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1720 w)

These 8 Evergreen Plants Make Your Porch Look Magical at Christmas – And They Stay Gorgeous All Winter

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that evergreens are often dismissed as quiet, supporting background players in the garden: solid green shrubs tucked along foundations while flamboyant perennials hog the limelight.
  • Growing real evergreen plants in containers can provide a brilliant Christmas display that continues looking attractive all winter.
  • Sources indicate that best of all, these container-friendly evergreens transition seamlessly from Christmas décor to winter curb appeal that lasts long after the holiday lights come down.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that evergreens are often dismissed as quiet, supporting background players in the garden: solid green shrubs tucked along foundations while flamboyant perennials hog the limelight. Yet when chosen thoughtfully, they can become show-stopping centerpieces. This is a time of year to celebrate the holiday season, but rather than relying on temporary displays, why not go for something with real staying power?

Growing real evergreen plants in containers can provide a brilliant Christmas display that continues looking attractive all winter. Flanking a front door or framing porch steps with holiday porch pots filled with living potted evergreens offers charm and longevity. Beyond classic deep emerald needles, today’s best container evergreens can deliver winter berries, flowers, contrasting textures, and even fragrance to greet guests as they arrive at your stoop.

Sources indicate that best of all, these container-friendly evergreens transition seamlessly from Christmas décor to winter curb appeal that lasts long after the holiday lights come down. With minimal upkeep, they lend easy elegance through the dark days of winter, then you can move them as needed to assist in decades-long displays. From trailing options to compact shrubs, here are 8 gorgeous evergreens you can use to transform your front porch into an enchanting holiday welcome.

Industry observers note that growing evergreens in containers unlocks wonderful design flexibility, allowing you to cluster different heights, trailing textures, and berry accents right at eye level near your doorway. However, while container-grown evergreens are generally easygoing and make great seasonal décor, they need a little more winter care than evergreens growing in the ground.

Because their potted roots sit above ground, they are more vulnerable to freezing temperatures and drying winter winds. It’s a good idea to choose evergreen varieties that are rated at least one or two USDA hardiness zones colder than your local climate, so plant roots have the best shot at surviving winter freezes unscathed.

It has been revealed that use frost-proof containers crafted from thick resin, fiberglass, glazed stoneware, or heavy wood. Avoid unglazed thin terracotta in cold climates, as trapped moisture will expand and crack clay walls. If your winters are very cold, consider wrapping the pots in burlap. Always leave unobstructed drainage holes and elevate your pots slightly on pot feet so icy water doesn't have a chance to pool underneath. You can buy Tortoise Pot Toes from Amazon to help ensure the best drainage.

Fill the containers with a coarse, fast-draining potting mix. Once you are past the holiday season and heading to spring, you can add a slow-release organic fertilizer. Even in winter, evergreens continue losing moisture through their foliage. Check the soil every couple of weeks and water deeply whenever the top two inches (5cm) feel dry and temperatures are above freezing. You’re now ready to add some of these evergreens to make your porch sparkle during Christmas and shine all winter long….

Alberta spruce is a classic choice for a Christmas tree, but most are large. If you fancy flanking your front door with classic, miniature Christmas trees, dwarf Alberta spruce (Picea glauca ‘Conica’) is perfect for a pot. Hardy across zones 3-8, this conifer naturally grows into a dense, velvety green, symmetrical cone, so it requires zero shearing to maintain its crisp silhouette. Also, because it adds just 2-4 inches (5-10cm) of growth per year, it thrives in a generous 14-18-inch (35-45cm) container for years, before needing upsizing or transplanting into the yard.

Place in full sun to light afternoon shade, rotating every few weeks. Keep the potting mix evenly moist but sharply drained, and mist occasionally. For a little extra holiday magic, underplant with trailing wintergreen or variegated ivy. Avoid heavy ornaments that might bend the fine branch tips. You can buy Dwarf Alberta Spruce from Nature Hills at a 30% discount. Add a couple for a lovely, symmetrical entryway feature.

Boxwood (Buxus spp.) brings classic English-garden elegance to winter porches in zones 5-9. Its dense clusters of small, glossy leaves stay green through sub-freezing weather. For containers, choose compact, cold-hardy cultivars such as Green Velvet (which forms a lush, rounded mound) or Green Gem. You can buy Brighter Blooms Green Velvet Boxwood from Walmart. Alternatively, go for pre-trained pyramid and globe topiaries for instant architectural polish.

Place potted boxwoods in partial shade to full sun. In northern zones, shelter them from harsh afternoon winter sun and drying winds. Plant in well-drained potting soil, and water deeply when unfrozen soil dries out. Dress for the holidays with velvet ribbon bows or tuck crimson winterberry stems into the soil around the base. Save any light shaping shears for late spring after the risk of last frost is passed.

In a recent development, nothing reveals the arrival of Christmas quite like holly (Ilex spp.), with its glossy leaves and scarlet berries. While towering tree hollies promptly outgrow porch pots, compact shrub cultivars thrive in containers in zones 5-9. Look for dwarf selections such as Little Red or compact Japanese Helleri. Alternatively, try deciduous winterberry Berry Poppins. Buy Proven Winners Berry Poppins Winterberry Holly from Plant Addicts for a container-sized beauty loaded with vibrant berry clusters.

In a recent development, just remember that hollies are dioecious. To enjoy berries, you need a female cultivar paired near a compatible male (such as Mr Poppins for winterberry). Failing that, buy a nursery pot where both sexes are planted together. Grow hollies in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic potting mix. Keep berries safely out of reach of pets, and enjoy watching winter songbirds visit as spring approaches.

If your front porch sits beneath a deep overhang or faces north where sun-loving conifers struggle, Japanese skimmia (Skimmia japonica) is a revelation. Hardy in zones 6-8, this neat, mounded broadleaf evergreen thrives in partial to full shade, retaining leathery, aromatic leaves all year. Better still, it delivers multi-season magic: in fall and early winter, male cultivars like Rubella produce clusters of flower buds that last right through Christmas, before opening into fragrant spring blossoms, while female varieties like Reevesiana bear true red berries.

According to recent reports, plant skimmia in an acidic, humus-rich potting mix (such as an ericaceous blend) with sharp drainage. Water regularly during dry spells, using rainwater if your tap water is hard. Nestle pots in a sheltered porch corner that is protected from icy gales. You can buy Skimmia Male Plants from Plant Addicts for shade-loving beauty to bedazzle on a covered porch. Add pinecones and ribbons to make pots festive.

Industry observers note that also known as eastern teaberry or boxberry, American wintergreen (Gaultheria procumbens) is a low-growing native evergreen groundcover. But it punches above its compact 6-inch (15cm) height in winter containers. Hardy in zones 3-8, its shiny, oval leaves transform over winter, from deep green to mahogany-bronze in cold weather. This provides a gorgeous backdrop for large, glossy red berries that cling to the stems all winter long.

Because it trails gracefully over pot rims, it makes a lovely festive spiller around the base of dwarf spruce, boxwood, or winterberry stems in mixed holiday planters. Give it a spot in partial to full shade. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic potting soil. Keep soil consistently damp and avoid lime-heavy fertilizers. You can buy Arbor Day Foundation Store’s Wintergreen Teaberry Pot Plants from Amazon in triple packs. Perfect under a porch cover, awning, or larger tree or shrub.

Recent findings suggest that goldcrest cypress aka Goldcrest Monterey cypress (Hesperocyparis macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’) is also sold as lemon cypress, and it lives up to its names in winter porches. Hardy in zones 7-10 (and also enjoyed as a cool-room or sheltered patio container specimen in colder zones), this upright conifer is filled with chartreuse-gold foliage that releases a zesty aroma when you brush past it. You can buy Wonderland Flora’s Lemon Cypress Goldcrest Wilma Plants from Walmart in packs of four.

Industry observers note that its narrow, columnar shape fits neatly into tight entryway corners and pairs symmetrically beside front doors. Grow Goldcrest in full sun to intensify its golden hues, and plant in a fast-draining potting mix. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry, but don’t let roots sit in soggy saucers. Dress the pot base with pinecones and burgundy ribbon for a contemporary holiday look that keeps sparkling into spring.

If you need to soften the edges of a structured winter pot, add some cascading English ivy (Hedera helix). Hardy in zones 4-9, this classic vining evergreen offers lobed emerald or crisp cream-and-gold variegations. Try cultivars like Glacier and Goldchild to brighten shady entryways with ease. While it can be invasive in the ground, it thrives in containers. Plant around the lip of mixed planters with upright boxwood or red-berried skimmia, or train up a wire obelisk for vertical interest.

In a recent development, ivy thrives in partial to full shade, and prefers slightly drier, well-drained potting soil. Overwatering in winter is the main enemy. Just snip stray runners occasionally to keep trails tidy, and never allow stems to root into surrounding masonry. You can buy Glacier Ivy from Plant Addicts for trailing creams and greens to add lush, lively winter movement.

If you want guests to pause in delight at your front door, plant sweet box (Sarcococca confusa). Hardy in zones 6-9, this understated, slow-growing broadleaf evergreen features dense, pointed leaves that look refined all year. What makes it unique for holiday decorating is that it flowers in winter. Depending on where you garden, you’ll have either buds or open flowers on this evergreen shrub at Christmas time. As a bonus, these creamy flowers are sweetly fragrant even on chilly days.

Industry observers note that sweet box thrives in deep to partial shade and prefers shelter from winds, so a covered front porch or courtyard alcove is ideal. Plant in a medium-sized container filled with rich, well-drained, neutral-to-slightly-acidic potting mix. Keep soil evenly moist when unfrozen. Minimal pruning is required: simply snip a few fragrant sprigs to tuck into holiday vases. You can buy Hirt’s Gardens Sweet & Lo Sweet Box Plants from Amazon for a shade-loving evergreen that fills entryways with honey scent.

Industry observers note that mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

Sources indicate that the concept is playful, but its purpose is practical. A standard adoption photograph may show what a dog looks like; a creative profile offers another reason to stop scrolling and learn more about the animal behind the image.

Someone might come for the art and leave wanting a dog. Turns out, the best thing in the gallery might have four legs and be up for adoption.

The Sato Project rescues dogs in Puerto Rico and helps place them in homes, including in the northeastern United States. Some arrive with limited information about their histories, and assumptions about a dogâs background can influence how potential adopters perceive them.

Industry observers note that dogs also see color differently from humans. People typically have three types of color-sensitive cone cells in their retinas, while dogs have two, a form of vision known as dichromacy. Dogs distinguish blues and yellows relatively well but have more difficulty differentiating reds and greens. Their visual experience of the world is therefore different from ours.

That doesnât mean dogs see the world in black and white. Color is only one possible influence on how they respond to an object. Shape, contrast, texture, scent, movement, and the surrounding environment may also play a part.

A sculpture might have us admiring its color and form. The dog? They might be more interested in giving it a sniff. Different critics, different criteria.

Sources indicate that although the profiles are not scientific personality assessments or guarantees of compatibility, they do invite us to learn more about each dog. Conversations with the rescue team and time spent meeting the dog remain essential to finding a suitable match.

In a recent development, rescue work involves far more than finding adopters. Veterinary care, foster placements, transportation, behavioral support, and follow-up all require time and resources. Helping the public connect with the dogs is only one part of that work, but an important one.

A member of the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae), the pumpkin is a cultivated squash, technically a fruit, with both savory and sweet culinary applications. While some countries wouldnât dare serve a roast dinner without a generous helping beside their potatoes, in the US, the nutritious pumpkin is usually relegated to seasonal decorations or the key ingredient in the eponymous pie.

Industry observers note that there are more than 100 varieties of pumpkin with slightly different textures, flavors, and recipe applications. What they all have in common is that they are low in calories, high in antioxidants, rich in vitamins & minerals, and, when prepared correctly, safe for dogs to eat.

Compared with the potato, a vegetable commonly used in both human and canine recipes, the pumpkin is higher in fiber, much lower in carbohydrates, and is far more digestible. It is often included in diets for cats and dogs with digestive problems due to its beneficial impact on intestinal health and function.

Even the seeds of certain pumpkin varieties, when properly prepared, have been found to help eliminate intestinal parasites.1.

In a recent development, and the cherry atop this pumpkin pie? Most dogs find the taste of pumpkin irresistible.

In a recent development, though there are certainly some dogs that challenge this notion, we shouldnât use our dogs as an eco-friendly alternative waste disposal unit. Yes, pumpkin is a safe and healthy food we can share with dogs, but there are some dos, donâts, and precautions to be aware of.

Pumpkin is a delicious, healthy, and nutritious food that deserves to be seen as more than just a Halloween decoration or pie ingredient. Dogs love the taste, and their digestive systems will thank you.

For years, business owners and property managers have wrestled with the same question: how do you tell the difference between a legitimate service animal and a pet that someone is trying to pass off as one?

Itâs a question John Bradford spent years trying to answer, first as a property manager overseeing thousands of rental units, and now as the founder of PetScreening, a platform used to verify animal accommodation requests across more than 7 million rental units nationwide.

With the rising number of service dogs and emotional support animals leading to incidents of confusion, conflict, and exploitation, John sets the record straight on how to verify a real service animal from one that isn't, and what you are legally allowed to ask.

Industry observers note that the truth is that most people donât fully understand the laws around service animals and emotional support animals, and even well-meaning questions can come across as anything but. That gray area and confusion can create real risk. Ask the wrong question, and a business can face a discrimination complaint. Ask no questions at all, and policies and rules become easy to bend, which leads to potentially dangerous situations.

Getting this right protects everyone involved, including the people who genuinely rely on these animals every day.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), service animals are defined as:.

âDogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities.â.

Sources indicate that disabilities vary widely, from physical and sensory to psychiatric, intellectual, and neurological. The needs of each person are different, so the trained tasks may look different from person to person. The ADA cites that the service animal must be a dog or, in rare cases, a miniature horse. Federal law does not require certifications, registrations, vests, or ID cards for these animals.

Beyond the specification that the animal must be trained to perform tasks, the legal standard is limited, so it can be difficult to easily identify which animals are legitimately service dogs and which are not. This is where public confusion starts.

There are plenty of ways to make a dog look like a service animal, like labeled vests, âregistrationâ certifications, and IDs, but none of these are federally supported. A dog wearing a vest isnât automatically a service animal, and a dog without one isnât automatically a pet. What matters legally is not appearance or paperwork. Itâs the dogâs trained ability to perform certain tasks.

In a recent development, this is the distinction many find hardest to grasp, and it matters because different laws apply to each. Service dogs are protected under the ADA and, due to their training and the tasks they perform, they are permitted in public spaces such as restaurants, retail stores, and hotels. That could mean guiding someone who is visually impaired, alerting an owner to an oncoming seizure, or reminding them to take medication. Service animals are also protected under the Fair Housing Act and require paperwork if the disability or need for the animal is not obviously understood.

In a recent development, emotional support animals (ESAs) are different. Their value comes from the comfort their presence provides. They donât necessarily have to be dogs, they arenât required to be trained to perform specific tasks, and theyâre not covered by the ADA to be allowed in public spaces like restaurants.

They are, however, protected by the Fair Housing Act. Under this, landlords are generally required to make allowances for an ESA if a tenant has appropriate documentation from a licensed healthcare provider establishing a disability-related need. Examples of disabilities warranting an ESA include, but are not limited to, anxiety disorders or autism.

Industry observers note that ESA accommodations are supposed to come through legitimate means, typically an established relationship with a licensed medical or mental health professional who can document the need. But some people have found loopholes for this by filling out forms online or paying fees for instant letters, which only fuels public skepticism about the legitimate need for these animals. Not to mention, this abuse can make people wary of service dogs, too.

In a recent development, while there is no foolproof visual test, trained service animals typically display consistent, recognizable behaviors. These dogs show exemplary discipline and obedience to the commands of their handler. They have the ability to ignore external distractions from other dogs, people, food, sounds, and smells while focusing on the needs of their handler. They display a calm temperament and are not aggressive or anxious. It is also expected that these animals be quiet, unless they are tasked with alerting an owner to a medical issue, and that they are housebroken and trained to walk on a leash without unnecessary pulling or circling.

This is where business owners and landlords need to tread carefully. When it isnât obvious that a dog is a service animal, staff are permitted to ask:.

Is this dog required because of a disability?

What task has it been trained to perform?

Thatâs the full extent of it. Staff should not ask about the nature of a personâs disability, demand documentation or proof of training, or require dogs to demonstrate their tasks. Asking beyond the two questions, even if it comes from a place of genuine curiosity or caution, can expose a business to discrimination claims.

News stories about supposed service animals harming bystanders in public continue to raise questions about the legitimacy of those animals, and businesses are often caught in the crossfire. These incidents are symptoms of a larger problem: businesses and property owners navigating without clear guidance, while people with legitimate needs are met with suspicion.

Service animals and emotional support animals play an essential role in the lives of the people who rely on them, and protecting that role starts with understanding the rules.

Industry observers note that if you own a business or manage a property, you donât need to become legal experts overnight, but you do need a consistent, fair process that respects peopleâs rights and keeps everyone safe. When everyone knows where the lines are, the people who truly depend on these animals can go about their lives without facing doubt at every door.
